utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me immediately concede I accept that we didn't make the objection I'm about to make in relation to some of the examinations conducted by my learned friends who defend. However, that question invited speculation. The answer of the witness was entirely speculative. And in our submission, the Court should curtail any speculation on the part of the witness. There appears to be an attempt by a number of counsel to turn him into some kind of quasi expert. To be fair to Mr. Thayer, in the last set of questions, the ones that objections were taken to by others, Mr. Thayer tried to do the precise opposite and he tried to make it clear to the witness he was after his personal view and his personal recollection. If the witness has a personal recollection of things that have been put to him, then we say fair enough; but if not, speculation should be curtailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Josse. What's your comment to that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can just simply put the question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, he answered you I don't know, and from then onwards he was trying to give some kind of thought of his how this could be explained. But where does it get you?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can move along, Mr. President. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- if you look at the next paragraph Commander Zivanovic describes the line of contact with the enemy as including Kamenica, Suceska, Cerska, and by the Bratunac Brigade along Kravica, Bratunac to Zuti Most, and Sase. And if we look a little further down he says: "We will try to cut the Zeleni Jadar-Zepa road in the course of the following day." Sir, does this document jog your memory at all about whether the VRS, and particularly the Drina Corps, was experiencing military successes during this period of time in overtaking these locations listed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident that the Drina Corps did have some successes. In view of the fact that in 1992 and 1993 in these areas a lot had been happening in terms of unilateral actions on the part of the 28th Division. Maybe at the time that was not its name, that was not what it was known as, but in any case the BiH army in Srebrenica inflicted losses on the Serbian population in the area. And this could no longer be tolerated. This behaviour of the Srebrenica units could no longer be tolerated. Something had to be done to protect the population, and this operation was aimed at saving the Serbian population in the area of Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the months just prior to your taking command of the Guards Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer. Are you leaving this document? Are you finished --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're finished with that document, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one question I would like to put. I will refer the witness to the last paragraph of that document which reads in the English version: "We will completely adhere to your proposal from the points 3 and 4 in keeping with your document strictly confidential number 171-05/1." Does that mean anything to you, Mr. Lazic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to know that. I was in the Main Staff and this is correspondence between the Drina Corps and the Uzice Corps, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it mean to you that there had been previous correspondence between the Drina Corps and the Uzice unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging from what I can read here, there was but I can't say that for a fact because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Thayer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you took command of the Guards Brigade in May of 1993, the 21st, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in fact in the months just prior to you taking command of that brigade, your brigade, the Guards Brigade, played an important role in these actions across this area of the Podrinje, this Operation Proboj. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see 65 ter 3369, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S, please. And in the B/C/S if we could scroll down a little bit, and, sir, I have a hard copy if that will be easier for you, but that's good right there. This is a Srpska Vojska issue from January of 1994 in which the successes of the Guards Brigade are recounted in your interview. If we look at this section, and let me direct your attention to the portion which starts: "The commander of this elite unit Milenko Lazic says: 'The order to form our brigade was issued already in mid-December 1992 and all the preparations were completed by the 19th January, which is why we commemorate the 12th night as the day of our unit. And it is actually the RS in small. We share with our young country all its problems and the successes too. This is a manoeuvre, an assault, and a strong artillery brigade. We have executed all our orders in time achieved great results and we are going to continue to do so and it must never be forgotten. It is our natural right to possess all of the Serbian territory.'" Were you quoted accurately there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is that an accurate recitation of your unit's successes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe there was a bit of propaganda in there, some things may have been painted in somewhat brighter colours, but the journalist was correct for most of the -- most of the article is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, the unit had successes in Cerska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before my arrival at the unit, the unit was active in the area of Cerska and was successful in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And successful in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Skelani. I apologise for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were there successes in Skelani, colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I arrived in the unit I remember it had had a very unfavourable situation in Ratkovici village. An operative officer of the brigade was taken prisoner with another two soldiers. Up until the present day their fate is not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand why that would stick out in your mind, but you did -- your unit did have successes in Skelani and then in Srebrenica and Gorazde and Zepa during this operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not believe that this unit may be described as the witness's unit in this context because the successes that the Prosecutor mentions happened way before the witness arrived in this unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go on. I think that is -- the question perfectly fits what is contained in that paragraph read from the Vojska -- whatever the name of the paper is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Srpska Vojska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Srpska Vojska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you want me to repeat the question or did you understand the question? Your unit did have successes in Skelani, Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa in the earlier months of 199 --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no successes in Srebrenica because the unit did not enter Srebrenica. It also had nothing to do with Zepa and at that time it had nothing to do with Gorazde either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know what happened to the Muslim populations that had been living in Konjevic Polje and Cerska and Kamenica during this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period of time when the area was being liberated, I wasn't there. I suppose the populace went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I understand you weren't on the ground, but being in the Main Staff and being in the area of Eastern Bosnia, sir, do you suppose or do you know where those Muslim civilians went as a result of Operation Proboj?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I'm not sure and I don't know it for certain; however, I suppose that all of them must have moved to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, trying to avoid Mr. Josse rising to object, this is to an extent speculation. So let's try to avoid as much speculation as possible. Mr. Lazic, you either know -- you either have an answer to the question or you don't. We don't want you to speculate. If you don't know exactly what happened, just say: I don't know what happened, I can't answer that question, and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one more --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one more question on this topic, sir. Do you recall that that's, in fact, exactly what happened, that the people were forced into Srebrenica and that created a humanitarian disaster in March and April of 1993? Do you recall hearing about that at the time, that people had been forced and compressed, crammed into the urban area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that things went along the lines you described concerning Srebrenica, but before that some 100 villages inhabited by Serbs had been driven out, houses set on fire, and losses inflicted upon the civilians by the 28th Division and the units in Srebrenica. What followed was a consequence of the events before the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that in your recollection Zepa had not been a successful object of the VRS as a result of Operation Proboj. Is that your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention the VRS. I mentioned the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Colonel. Now, with respect to your time in the Main Staff of the VRS, do you recall whether or not the VRS had achieved any military successes with respect to Zepa before you assumed command of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So as not to be forced to speculate, I can tell you that I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at 65 ter 2742, please. Now, this is a somewhat lengthy document, sir. I have hard copy if that would be more convenient for you to review. And please take your time, Colonel. Again, as I said, I don't want you to feel rushed. Are you ready to proceed, sir? In the interests of trying to save some time, I'll just ask you a couple of questions about this document. This is a Main Staff combat order for the liberation of Zepa and Gorazde dated May 1st of 1993. Did you see that this was drafted by General Miletic, then Colonel Miletic? Did you see that, sir? It's on the last page if you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you look at page 2 of the English - and that's on the first page of your document, sir - do you see where it refers to the Muslims' military defeats in Kamenica, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember this combat order, this plan to liberate Zepa and Gorazde, part of which was to be commanded by General Miletic? Do you recall this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, do you recall about this operation in terms of its implementation? Do you recall whether it ever got off the ground, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These successes were achieved in the previous offensive or operation. The goals to liberate Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde were not fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, let's turn to another document. This is 65 ter 3177. This is the last document I want to show you along these lines, Colonel, before we turn to something else. Let us know when you're ready to have the document scrolled down to continue reading. And I do have a hard copy if that is easier.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to read the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then I'd kindly ask Madam Usher to hand up the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime while he reads, is there any special part of this document that you wish to direct the witness to; in which case I would ask the technicians to zoom to that section and the accused will be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. We can go straight away to the bottom of page 2 in the English, which is page 2 of the B/C/S but towards the top of that version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the section that I just noted where the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic, in this 4 July 1994 report for his brigade says: "We have won the war in Podrinje but we have not beaten the Muslims completely, which is what we must do in the next period. We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the English version we need to go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: " ... the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task, the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. There will be no retreat. When it comes to the Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realizing that they cannot survive there." Now, sir, you knew Colonel Ognjenovic and later served with him in the Drina Corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you aware in 1994 when you were in the Main Staff or in 1995 -- I'm sorry, in 1992 to 1993 when you were in the Main Staff or in 1995 when you served together in the Drina Corps command that Colonel Ognjenovic had set these objectives for his brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness answered but I do not understand how could have the witness knew in 1992 and 1993 of something that somebody would have said in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Entirely correct. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can clarify the question for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and still the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In 1994 when this document was authored by Commander Ognjenovic and when you later served with him in the Drina Corps command, did you come to know that he had set these goals for his brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But as we've seen in the documents and as you've testified, I believe, is there anything inconsistent in this report by Commander Ognjenovic from what you understood the goals of the VRS during these operations beginning in 1992 that we talked about all the way through here 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question, Your Honour - it again requires the witness to speculate - for the very simple reason that something can be contradictory only if it is said or done by two people at the same time. The witness said he wasn't aware of this document and now the Prosecutor is asking him whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, stop. There is a limit beyond which you cannot go when you raise -- rise to make an objection. Mr. Lazic, please answer the question if you can. If you're not in a position to answer it, then tell us so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat the question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would suggest you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, as we've seen in the documents and as you've testified, is there anything inconsistent in this report by Commander Ognjenovic from what you understood to be the goals of the VRS during these operations, which as we've seen began in 1992 and continued all the way up to where we are now, which is 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 I wasn't of the opinion that Ognjenovic stated. I thought that the Serbian people were endangered because there was a lack of tolerance in terms of ethnic make-up and religious affiliation. I believed it would lead to a separation along the ethnic and religious lines. I also believed that that could be a solution of the conflicts which were created in Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995. I never said that that excluded any co-existence if possible. If not, then probably they have to go their own ways. In any case, what he said is something I would not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just said at the end of your answer: If co-existence isn't possible, then probably they have to go their own ways. What do you mean by that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say that if co-existence was impossible and if that is proven by the situation in the field, then, just like General Milovanovic wrote in the previous document, the Serbian population should be enabled to live in the territory it did and the Muslim people to live in the territory they lived at. This was not a goal or an intent to do that at any cost. Once it is established that there are no other possibilities, i.e., there was no possibility of a life together, then one needs to come up with solutions. This is how I see the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what are those solutions, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again you'll tell me I'm speculating. I didn't deal with such issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not believe that this is an appropriate question for this witness. This witness is not an expert witness and he cannot answer, therefore, to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, he's living experiences -- he's testifying on experiences that he lived through as a military man at the time. So please go ahead, but we don't need any speculation, we don't want any speculation from Mr. Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, as the President of the Chamber just said, in your lived experience and as a military officer during this time, in these locations did you find during this period of time from 1992 to 1994 that this co-existence that you spoke about became impossible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have the feeling that the Serb side was not to blame for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood that those are your feelings, sir. And looking at this document that Commander Ognjenovic wrote, isn't it the case that when he says: "We have won the war in Podrinje but we have not beaten the Muslims completely. We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje ..." that's what he's talking about, isn't it, that that hope for co-existence, in his eyes, was lost?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think it was appropriate to answer. It would be interpreted as what he feels, his feelings, and if he asked this question what somebody else thought, I don't think it's appropriate. Perhaps one should call in Colonel Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam Fauveau. Let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's time for the break anyway. Change the subject, in other words, Mr. Thayer. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's move to a new subject, Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. And just to advise the Court, I've greatly reduced the rest of my planned examination. I think I will take Colonel Lazic up to the rest of the day today, maybe a little bit into tomorrow. It took a little longer than I expected, but I was able to really cut down the examination. So I think we'll be able to come in pretty close to the three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 203.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good afternoon again, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the document we started the morning out with, and I just wanted to ask you a couple of questions about one particular section and then we'll move on. And I have a hard copy, with Madam Usher's assistance. Colonel, I direct your attention to page 3 of your document, and we'll be looking at section 2: "Tasks of the Drina Corps." I just want to ask you two or three questions about this one section. Do you see where it says: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa"? Did you see that section, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is towards the end of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you would agree that that language sounds a lot like the language from the Ognjenovic report that we were just looking at before the break? You would agree with me, sir, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you draft this section, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps tasks are copied from the directive number 7 that was valid at the time. They are copied word for word from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I understand, sir, as you sit here today do you have any knowledge as how -- as to how the Main Staff or the Supreme Command came up with this language that we saw in this previous Bratunac Brigade report? Do you have any knowledge how that language made it into directive 7, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the answer to your question because I don't know who the author of these words is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience serving on the Main Staff and in your experience in the VRS, do you know which organ or which department would have come up with that language for directive 7, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was customary for these items of the orders or directives relative to the tasks of the subordinate units to be drafted by the commander or possibly from the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are you referring, sir, to the commander or possibly Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about directives, then the Main Staff; if we're talking about orders, then the command subordinated to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm talking about this specific language in the directive. Which department or organ would in your experience have been tasked to come up with that portion of the directive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has just answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked him to clarify when he said that it was customary for those items of the orders or directives relative to the tasks to be drafted by the commander. I asked him if it was the commander of the Main Staff or the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, and his answer to that question was: If we're talking about directives, then the Main Staff; if we're talking about orders, then the command subordinated to the corps command. So I'm afraid that his answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's told you that if you're talking of a directive, it's directed to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Then I'll follow-up with one final question on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff is responsible for authoring that section, who would assist him in your experience with drafting that language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is speculation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not speculation --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this is not the Chief of Staff who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question, please. Go ahead, Mr. Lazic, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that in this kind of work, the only people who could assist were those who had the expertise, i.e., if it's the commander or the Chief of Staff who performs this job, nobody else can help them. The only thing that can be done is to do his leg work for him and take that draft to the typist to type it up. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony then that if the Chief of Staff is drafting this language that we're looking at, that there is no other input in your experience from any other member of the Chief of Staff's staff, any of his subordinates, who assist him other than a typist? Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you testified yesterday - and this is at the beginning of page 35 - that you can't remember a 25 May 1995 VRS shelling attack on Srebrenica, which was memorialized in a report from the artillery chief of the Bratunac Brigade to the Drina Corps. Do you remember that testimony yesterday, sir? We need an audible answer, I'm sorry, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let me see if I can help jog your memory about the events of that day. Do you recall that at approximately 1630 hours that day NATO executed air-strikes which destroyed two bunkers and an ammunition depot in Pale. Do you remember that happening, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall that soon after those NATO air-strikes the VRS took 200 UN peacekeeper hostages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm sure, sir, you're referring to the pictures, the video-clips, of UN personnel being chained to various military facilities. Is that what you're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood. And what you saw on TV, sir, was the UNPROFOR personnel being chained to various military installations or facilities by the VRS; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, sir, that on that same day that all this was happening, in addition to the shells being fired on Srebrenica that the VRS shelled Sarajevo and Tuzla where 130-millimetre shell injured 200 and killed 70 young people who were celebrating Tito's birthday and Youth Day in Tuzla. Do you remember that happening, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I will let you go ahead, but what's the relevance of this now?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The relevance, sir, Mr. President, is -- and actually if I may ask the witness just to remove his headphones for my answer, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he understand English in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't know. I've not met him previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazic, do you understand English? Do you understand English, Mr. Lazic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you remove your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm simply trying to orient the witness's recollection to this particular day which he has indicated previously and in his testimony he simply can't recall. So I'm going through these significant events to see if that will help him recall or not certain other events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But you have advanced far already. So let's put the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to show you two documents and then I'll put my question to you. The first is 65 ter 3358. As we can see, this is a very urgent report from the artillery chief of the Bratunac Brigade, Mico Gavric, to the Drina Corps command and it's dated 25 May 1995. In it he says that: "At 1907 hours we opened fire on Srebrenica on Colonel Lazic's orders." Sir, are you aware of any other Colonel Lazic in the Drina Corps command? And I don't mean to be facetious when I ask that question. Are you aware of any other Colonel Lazic in the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear of any other Colonel Lazic in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the next document I'd like to show you is 65 ter 3359. We can see this is an interim combat report from Commander Blagojevic to the Drina Corps command. Paragraph 1: "In accordance with an oral order from Colonel Lazic we fired two shells from two 105-millimetre howitzers, a total of four shells, on the town of Srebrenica at 1907 hours. Artillery observers at Pribicevac reported that two shells fell near the Domavija feature. The other two shells were not observed but they fell on Srebrenica." Now, sir, you don't have any basis to doubt the authenticity of these records, do you? And I can show you the handwritten versions of these reports before they were finalised if you like.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you don't have any doubts that this shelling actually occurred on that day, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want you to think very carefully before you answer. Who gave you the order to pass on to the Bratunac Brigade to fire those shells?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness already answered to this question yesterday. I put him this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a cross-examination, so let him proceed, and I take it that there are more questions to follow. So, Mr. Lazic, please, if you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Already in 2004 in an interview given to your organs in Banja Luka I answered that question by saying approximately the following: I did not have the right to order -- to issue orders, and this is evident. I was not an organ who could issue orders. How come I mention -- my name is mentioned with regard to this order, given the fact that both of them were professional officers and knew very well that they were not supposed to receive orders from somebody who did not have the right to issue orders? How and what happened in the operations room and how the duty operations officer passed on the order referring to me and mentioning my name, I really wouldn't know. I only know that I did not have the right to issue this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, as standing in for the Chief of Staff were you in a position to pass on an order from a superior command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, he was representing the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was just to correct -- we have no evidence that on this specific day he was representing the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. We have no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps he can answer the question and we'll get the necessary information. Yes, Mr. Lazic. Perhaps you can -- yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not stand in for the Chief of Staff during that period of time because Colonel Krstic had already come to work and was performing his duties. So at the time I did not stand in for the Chief of Staff. There is proof to that effect. Yesterday evidence was shown in the form of a piece of document that was signed by Krstic on the 13th, meaning a few days before this shelling took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, isn't it a fact that you didn't even need to be standing in for the Chief of Staff to have passed on that order from your superior command to the Bratunac Brigade. You could have been instructed by your superior command at any time to pass on that order, and I'm not talking about issuing an order, sir, I'm talking about passing on an order to the Bratunac Brigade. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said it that I cannot remember such a possibility although I'm not ruling it out. I'm not ruling this out but I'm saying that I can't remember having passed this order personally on. I may have been in the operations room when the duty officer was passing on this order and he may have said something to the effect, Here you have Colonel Lazic here, so execute the order. That may have happened, but I don't have any recollection of that and that's why my answer was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just as a point of clarification, Colonel, as a matter of how the VRS and organized armies operate, isn't it the case that simply as chief of operations and training you would have been in a position to pass on such an order from your superior command to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally believe that if the Main Staff had issued an order to this effect then the order was passed either to the commander or the Chief of Staff. I don't believe that somebody would have looked for me to communicate the order to me and to ask for me to pass it on. That's why I'm saying that it is possible that I was in the operations room and that the duty officer said something to the effect, Here Pukovnik Lazic is here, and that's why my name is mentioned because the two senior reporting officers had to mention somebody who could have passed on the order. And I personally say and I repeat, I don't know how this could have occurred because I had not issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the Chamber's indulgence, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to turn your attention now to this meeting at the Drina Corps command where President Karadzic, as you testified, came and gave this order. Okay. Now, as I understand it you were the first to brief the president according to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to clear the record, you referred to someone's wife who was also present. Whose wife was present for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Karadzic's wife was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you were present for this entire meeting with President Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were sitting in that room I was there. When they left the room, I was not with them; so when they were outside that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I understand that when General Krstic showed the president out, you weren't with him. Is that -- that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that President Karadzic asked how long would you need to set off for Zepa. That's what we have in the transcript at page 20, and the answer was: "Three to five days, depending on what the objective was." And his response was: "Well, make it as short as possible"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, please tell the Trial Chamber in as much detail as you can remember as you sit here today exactly what the order was that came out of President Karadzic's mouth at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I have stated so far. The president asked: How much time will it take you to set off to Srebrenica -- you said Zepa and I say Srebrenica. And the answer was: Depending on the target or the objective, it will take us three to five days in preparations. And he said: Make it the shorter time. And while they were sitting in that room they did not go into any further details of that future activity. The conversation that ensued was informal. I don't know whether the reason is the fact that the others were present there, so he did not want to go into any details. Whether the president said anything else to Krstic as they were moving towards the vehicle, I don't know. So I never heard any other discussion with this with regard save for the words that I have already repeated for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any other communications between President Karadzic and General Krstic or General Zivanovic or anyone else at the Drina Corps concerning, as you've testified, his order to move on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, although I know that there is a possibility of direct telephone communication or via encrypted messages between President Karadzic and the corps commander or the Chief of Staff. So I really don't know whether they had some exchanges because I was not in their respective rooms so I am not able to answer this question in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you testified that immediately upon President Karadzic's departure General Krstic returned and gathered the staff and right away tasks were assigned, drafting begun and work was on its way to create what ultimately became the July 2nd Krivaja 95 combat order. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So let me just ask you again, see if you have any recollection. Other than asking how long it would take to get to Srebrenica, what do you recall President Karadzic saying about any active combat operations towards the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as I said, there was no further discussion in that room concerning the operation. There was no mention of any other military topics. I heard what I heard. The rest of the conversation was informal, there were questions about Krstic's leg and his health, but there was no further discussion on the upcoming tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, again, Colonel, how is it that the Drina Corps command was able to begin planning for this operation based on what President Karadzic, as you recalled, said during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously it is visible from the combat documents that General Krstic drew reference for the documents concerning that operation from directives 7 and 7/1. That was his basis. All that was needed then was an order to be sent out. If as far as I understood, the president ordered to go ahead with the task and he dealt with the format by taking pieces of information from relevant documents otherwise used to draft our combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony then, sir, that President Karadzic's order as far as you could understand it from what you saw in the meeting and from what you saw General Krstic doing and producing was that he was relying on directives 7 and 7/1 in fulfilling this order from President Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you agree that this order that you received was consistent with the goals that had been set out in directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that with directives 7 and 7/1 in place that by the time that President Karadzic came to the Drina Corps command, the Drina Corps command already had a very good idea of what it needed to do to move on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you were asked at page 38 yesterday if General Krstic informed the Main Staff of this order from President Karadzic and your answer was that: "I can't tell you that precisely because he had a direct line from his office to the Main Staff. I can't tell you if he informed the Main Staff in what way, but I presume that he did." Now, Colonel, when you were interviewed by the Beara Defence team on November 30th of last year, you said on the bottom of page 1, and this goes up to page 2 of the English and unfortunately I wasn't furnished with the B/C/S if there was a B/C/S, I don't know, if it was just taken in English. But the statement says that after Krstic saw Karadzic off, I quote here: "Krstic then ordered," and this is in English 65 ter 3376 if people want to follow along. "Krstic then ordered for the corps command to assemble and said that after an order is received from the supreme commander the corps will get on with the job. Immediately thereafter the VRS Main Staff was informed via telegram that a combat order had been received and subordinate commanders were ordered to come to the command the next day at 0800 hours." Colonel, I put it to you that your recollection six months ago was very precisely, that immediately upon receiving this order from President Karadzic that the Drina Corps informed the Main Staff by telegram. Do you have an explanation for your changed memory about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is not changed. If that is what I said six months ago, then it is so. As time goes by I seem to forget many details. I am not certain sitting here today of everything that had taken place. In any case, if I said that a telegram message was sent out, then it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, you also said in your statement to the Beara team - and this is at the top of page 2 of that document - that President Karadzic said during the meeting that: "Anything that is lacking, a request should be put in through the Main Staff and everything will be provided." Do you recall President Karadzic saying those words, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that Krstic said that we were short of ammunition, fuel, and food. The president responded by saying, Put in a request and you will be given everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of participation by the Main Staff, either the command staff -- I'll start there. Are you aware of the participation of the command staff of the Main Staff in the Krivaja 95 operation once that operation got underway? I'm not talking about the preparation that happened at the Drina Corps command, but once the active combat operations were underway, are you aware of the participation of the Main Staff command staff in assisting the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in the operation. I didn't see anyone. I did hear that General Mladic came there to the forward command post. I only heard that, but I didn't see any of the members of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown an exhibit by my learned friend from the Miletic team, 5D1110, and I won't ask that it be shown. That was General Krstic's order for an analysis of the Krivaja 95 and Stupcanica operation, the Srebrenica and Zepa operations respectively. That was an afteraction analysis; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think you contrasted that to some of the analysis that you participated in in terms of the Spreca 95 operation in the spring of 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference. Spreca 95 was carried out by two corps. Krivaja 95 was the result of the Drina Corps' actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Exactly. And the analysis that we were talking about with respect to Spreca 95, that occurred while that operation was still ongoing because the Main Staff had encountered problems implementing Spreca 95 and that required Main Staff officers to be sent forward and actually create a Main Staff forward command post, two of them, in fact, in the Zvornik area. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this afteraction report from General Krstic, do you recall responding to that afteraction report seeking an accounting of everyone's activities during the course of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That document requested specific responses to specific topics ordered by General Krstic. Do you recall whether or not you responded to account for your activities and the other actions and analyses that General Krstic ordered in that document? Do you remember whether or not you responded to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked to analyse. I briefed orally the Chief of Staff about what had taken place. The document was sent to brigade commands to carry out analyses at their levels. The brigade commands will probably mention what was done. Those that were on the western front would say that I came by to control and regarding the issues included in my task. So that is where you can find a reference concerning my coming over and inquiring about my tasks; however, I was never asked to carry out a separate analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm afraid the time has come.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have a couple more questions. I'll pick it up tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be prepared for the next witness tomorrow, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may, I'd prefer to look at the transcript tonight and see if there's one or two follow-ups that I might would need tomorrow morning rather than finishing it up now, if I may be granted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we'll have to adjourn to tomorrow. We'll continue tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
